title: Steering Autoregressive Music Generation with Recursive Feature Machines
one_liner: MusicRFM finds internal directions inside a frozen music model that correspond to musical properties such as notes or chords, then adds those directions during generation to steer the output without retraining the base model.
lead: Controlling a pre-trained music generator is hard because the usual control methods either retrain the full model, optimize a control signal at every generation step, or degrade audio quality by pushing too bluntly on the output. MusicRFM uses a different route. It studies how the model's hidden states change when a musical property changes, learns a direction in hidden-state space for that property, and then injects that direction during generation time. The base model stays frozen, the steering signal is lightweight, and the control can vary over time or combine several musical properties at once.

problem.h2: Music control usually changes too much or too little
paras: A next-step music model generates the next audio unit from the units generated so far. Once such a model is trained, it already contains internal structure for rhythm, harmony, instrumentation, and note transitions. The challenge is to influence one chosen property, such as the presence of a target note, without retraining the full model or damaging the rest of the musical structure.

Direct retraining is costly and often task-specific. Per-step optimization can be slow because a control objective has to be solved during generation itself. Output-level editing can also introduce artifacts because it acts after the model has already committed to an internal plan. The paper instead asks whether the control signal can be applied inside the model, where the next-step decision is formed.

callout.html: Learn interpretable hidden-state directions for musical concepts in a frozen model, then add those directions during generation time according to a chosen schedule.

steps.b: Collect hidden states from the frozen model
steps.text: Run the pretrained music generator and record internal intermediate values during generation.
Estimate directions in hidden-state space that correspond to target musical properties.
Decide when and how strongly to apply each direction during generation.
Add the learned direction to the model's hidden state during generation time.
Optionally apply several directions together so multiple musical properties are enforced at once.

paras: MusicRFM changes the hidden state used by the frozen music generator at generation time. It does not retrain the full model and does not optimize a new control variable at every step. Instead, it adds a precomputed concept direction to the model's internal representation as generation unfolds.
object.object: the hidden state trajectory during generation

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: concept direction strength
hidden.name: concept direction strength
paras: The central quantity is how strongly a chosen hidden-state direction increases the probability of the target musical property while preserving the rest of the sequence. If the direction is too weak, the target note or chord barely appears. If it is too strong, it can override prompt adherence and distort other musical structure.

The paper learns these directions with Recursive Feature Machines, which fit probes to the model's internal behavior rather than to the output alone. The result is an interpretable direction that can be scaled up, down, turned on only during chosen time spans, or combined with other directions.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark components that should remain active when the steering direction is useful and well-scaled.

reads.html: The steering direction must be strong enough to raise the target property and restrained enough to avoid overriding the rest of the music.
RFM probes identify interpretable concept directions in MusicGen hidden states, and those directions are re-injected during generation time with controllable strength and timing.

paras: A pretrained next-step music model already organizes its internal state so that different musical properties affect next-step probabilities. If a particular note, chord, or local structure is represented consistently inside the hidden state, then changing the hidden state along the corresponding direction changes the model's next-step probability pattern in a predictable way. This is more direct than output editing because the intervention happens before the next unit is sampled.

Recursive Feature Machines are used to estimate those directions from internal responses. The probe is lightweight, but it is trained to track how hidden-state changes connect to the target concept. Once that relationship is identified, the steering stage no longer needs to solve an optimization problem online. It simply adds the learned direction, scaled by a chosen coefficient, to the hidden state at the selected layer and time step.

Time-varying schedules matter because many musical properties are local rather than global. A user may want one note or chord to be emphasized during one segment and not elsewhere. Multiple-direction control also matters because music is structured by several coupled properties at once. Because the directions are learned separately and applied inside the hidden state, the method can combine them more cleanly than a blunt output-level control signal.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the target is note C and the learned concept direction is available from the probe.
At one generation step, set alpha_t = 0.0 and the model behaves exactly like the base model.
At a later step, set alpha_t = 0.8 and add 0.8 times the concept direction to the hidden state.
The next-step probabilities shift toward events associated with note C because the hidden state now moves in the learned direction for that concept.
If alpha_t is reduced again, the steering influence weakens without changing the frozen model weights.

math.note: This update matters because it gives direct control over when and how strongly a musical property is enforced.

bars.h2: What the result should look like

charts.title: Frozen model without steering
charts.note: The base model follows the prompt well but does not reliably express the target musical property.

charts.title: MusicRFM
charts.note: The target property rises sharply while prompt adherence stays close to the base model because the intervention changes internal control rather than retraining the whole generator.

items.b: A learned direction may mix several concepts.
items.html: If the probe does not isolate the target property cleanly, steering one note may also drag along unwanted chord or timbre changes, because the hidden-state direction is not perfectly disentangled.

items.b: Large steering strength can override the prompt.
items.html: If the scale is too high, the target concept can dominate the hidden state and reduce adherence to the original text prompt or earlier musical context.

items.b: Control may depend on where it is injected.
items.html: A direction learned at one layer may not transfer cleanly to another layer, because the representation of the musical concept changes across depth.

The method works best when the probe learns a clean concept direction, the steering scale is tuned for the target property, and the intervention is applied at layers and time spans where that property is represented clearly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a pretrained music generator and choose a simple target property such as the presence of one note or one chord class. Record hidden states from the frozen model, train a lightweight probe to estimate the concept direction, and compare unsteered generation against steered generation on the same prompts.

The demo should measure how often the target property appears, how much the prompt meaning changes, and whether the effect can be confined to chosen time ranges. A convincing result shows that hidden-state steering raises the target property because the intervention changes the next-step decision inside the model, while the base model weights stay frozen.
demo.closing: The core claim is established if the target musical property rises sharply with only a small change in prompt adherence.
